new.title: Climb to the Mémorial Interallié on Cointe hill
new.desc: After 1918 the Allied nations chose Liège, the first city to resist the invasion of 1914, as the site of their joint memorial. Antwerp architect Joseph Smolderen built a 75 metre tower and the church of the Sacré-Cœur on the hill of Cointe between 1928 and 1937, paid for by public and private subscriptions in the Allied countries.
new.tip: The esplanade is always open and looks down over Guillemins station and the Meuse. The tower itself only opens on a few special days a year, so do not count on going up.
new.q: Mémorial Interallié Cointe Liège

new.title: Board the old trams at the Musée des Transports en commun
new.desc: A hall in the Vennes district holds around forty restored vehicles that once carried Liège to work, from horse-drawn trams of 1875 to electric trams, trolleybuses and city buses. Enthusiasts founded the museum in 1985 to save them from the scrapyard, and three of the trams came from the Aachen network.
new.tip: The museum is open from March to the end of November, and at weekends and on public holidays only from 2 pm. It is a flat fifteen minute walk from La Boverie.
new.q: Musée des Transports en commun de Wallonie Rue Richard Heintz 9 Liège

new.title: Trace Liège's iron age at the Maison de la Métallurgie
new.desc: Liège grew rich on iron, steel and zinc, and this museum in the former Dothée factory tells that story across nine rooms and 2,500 square metres. You meet local industry figures such as John Cockerill and Zénobe Gramme alongside the tools and machines of the trade.
new.tip: It sits just across the water from the Médiacité and La Boverie, so it pairs well with either. Guided tours are offered in English if you ask ahead.
new.q: Maison de la Métallurgie et de l'Industrie Boulevard Raymond Poincaré 17 Liège

new.title: Ride the river shuttle down the Meuse
new.desc: From spring to autumn a small passenger boat works the Meuse through Liège like a bus, calling at six stops between Fragnée in the south and Coronmeuse in the north. The whole run takes about an hour and passes the Guillemins quays, La Boverie, the city centre and the historic heart by the Grand Curtius.
new.tip: You buy tickets on board: a couple of euros for the first stop and one more for each further stop, or a day pass if you want to hop on and off. It runs weekends only at the start of the season and almost daily in July and August.
new.q: Passerelle La Belle Liégeoise Quai de Rome Liège

new.title: Count your way through the Tripick beers at Guillemins
new.desc: Tripick is a Liège beer range whose names are simply numbers, from 4 up to 8. Its brasserie stands on Place des Guillemins, directly opposite Calatrava's station, and serves the series alongside brasserie food.
new.tip: A good plan while waiting for a train: order two different numbers and compare. Sit outside for a full view of the station roof.
new.q: Brasserie Le Tripick Place des Guillemins 1 Liège

new.title: Visit the house where Grétry was born
new.desc: André-Modeste Grétry, the opera composer whose statue stands in front of the Liège opera house, was born in 1741 in this small Louis XV house in Outremeuse. It opened as a museum in 1913 in the presence of King Albert I and shows documents, furniture and personal belongings from his life.
new.tip: It only opens from Friday to Sunday and costs very little; under 26s get in free, and so does everyone on the first Sunday of the month.
new.q: Musée Grétry Rue des Récollets 34 Liège

new.title: Eat Liège classics at Tchantchès et Nanesse
new.desc: This tavern in the heart of the self-declared Free Republic of Outremeuse is a temple of Liège folklore, named after the city's puppet hero and his wife. The kitchen sticks to regional cooking at modest prices, including rabbit cooked in the house Tchantchès beer and fondue made with Herve cheese.
new.tip: It is a short walk from the Tchantchès museum, so combine the two. The house beers are strong, so pace yourself.
new.q: Taverne Tchantchès Nanesse Rue Grande-Bêche 35 Liège

new.title: Explore the overgrown fort in the Parc de la Chartreuse
new.desc: On the hill above Amercœur the Dutch built a fort between 1817 and 1823, named after the Carthusian monastery that once stood nearby. It never played a real military role: it became a barracks in 1891, a prison for Belgian patriots in the First World War and was used by the American army from 1944, and today it is being swallowed by woodland.
new.tip: The paths of the park are open to all, but the old buildings are crumbling, so admire them from outside. Wear proper shoes, as the tracks get muddy.
new.q: Parc de la Chartreuse Liège

new.title: Taste craft beer on tap at Wild Lab
new.desc: Among the old mansions of Rue Hors-Château, Wild Lab is an address for modern craft beer, with fourteen taps that change often and blackboards listing food and events. Expect hazy IPAs and collaborations from small breweries rather than the usual abbey names.
new.tip: Beers are sold in small 25 cl glasses, which makes it easy to try several. Arrive around five to get a table before the after-work crowd.
new.q: Wild Lab Rue Hors-Château 14 Liège

new.title: Slip into the postmodern Cour Saint-Antoine
new.desc: Between 1978 and 1985 architect Charles Vandenhove rescued a run-down block between Rue Hors-Château and Rue des Brasseurs. He restored the 17th to 19th century houses, added new postmodern homes and joined the two with a quiet pedestrian square that you enter through covered passages.
new.tip: Look for the arched passage, called an arvô in Liège, on Rue Hors-Château. The square is a peaceful place to sit after climbing the Montagne de Bueren nearby.
new.q: Cour Saint-Antoine Liège

new.title: Watch the marionettes at the Théâtre Al Botroûle
new.desc: Jacques Ancion and his wife opened this tiny puppet theatre at the foot of Rue Hocheporte in 1973, and with barely 42 seats it is as intimate as theatre gets. The repertoire mixes Liège classics starring Tchantchès and Nanesse with other texts, and since 2023 the house has been run by Elisabeth Ancion and the film maker Bouli Lanners.
new.tip: Shows are not daily, so check the programme and reserve, as the room fills fast. Some evenings are aimed at adults rather than children.
new.q: Théâtre Al Botroûle Rue Hocheporte 3 Liège

new.title: Go under Place Saint-Lambert at the Archéoforum
new.desc: Beneath the paving of Place Saint-Lambert lies an archaeological site of 3,725 square metres, opened in 2003. It stacks 9,000 years of settlement in one place: prehistoric finds, a Gallo-Roman villa, a Merovingian church and the successive cathedrals of Saint-Lambert.
new.tip: The entrance is easy to miss, down on the square itself. It is a good refuge on a wet day and takes about an hour.
new.q: Archéoforum Place Saint-Lambert Liège

new.title: Spend an evening at the Opéra Royal de Wallonie
new.desc: Liège's opera house is one of the three great opera houses of Belgium and has played in the same theatre since it was inaugurated in 1820. King William of Orange gave the city the land and the materials of a former Dominican convent on condition that a theatre be built there.
new.tip: The statue in front is the composer Grétry, a son of the city. Book well ahead for popular operas, as the cheaper seats go first.
new.q: Opéra Royal de Wallonie Place de l'Opéra Liège

new.title: Have lunch on the terrace of Brasserie Sauvenière
new.desc: The Grignoux, Liège's art-house cinema group, run this big brasserie next to their Sauvenière cinema on Place Xavier Neujean. The menu leans on organic and regional produce with vegetarian choices, and the large shaded terrace is surprisingly quiet for the city centre.
new.tip: They do not take reservations, so come a little before noon. A combined ticket gives you a meal, a coffee and a film on the same day.
new.q: Brasserie Sauvenière Place Xavier Neujean 12 Liège

new.title: Sit down to a no-frills plate at L'Industrie
new.desc: L'Industrie on Rue Saint-Gilles is the kind of plain neighbourhood restaurant where Liège eats its own cooking. The menu is boulets of course, but also steaks, chips and salads, served in a simple and friendly room.
new.tip: Bring cash in case cards are not accepted. It is a short walk from the cathedral and the Carré.
new.q: L'Industrie Rue Saint-Gilles 6 Liège

new.title: Play chess over a local beer at La Casa Ponton
new.desc: On the corner of Rue de la Cité and the old shopping lane En Neuvice, this busy café has chess and draughts tables and photos of Liège's industrial past on the walls. Around ten draught beers come largely from small breweries of the region, such as Tripick, Badjawe and Prieuré de Beaufays.
new.tip: It is two minutes from La Batte, so it works well after the Sunday market. It is a place for drinks, so eat before or after.
new.q: La Casa Ponton Rue de la Cité 7 Liège

new.title: Drink abbey beer at the Abbaye du Val-Dieu
new.desc: Cistercian monks founded Val-Dieu in 1216 in what they called an uncultivated and uninhabited corner of the Berwinne valley, in the Pays de Herve. The last three monks left in 2001, but the abbey lives on with a lay community, a brewery and a café, the Casse-Croûte, where you can eat and drink inside the abbey.
new.tip: The Casse-Croûte and the shop, which sells the abbey's beers and cheeses, are open every day. Signposted walks start right opposite the abbey.
new.q: Abbaye du Val-Dieu Aubel

new.title: Brave real Herve cheese at the Fromagerie du Vieux Moulin
new.desc: Herve is the only Belgian cheese with a protected designation of origin, and it is famous for its strong smell. This small dairy on the Herve plateau is known as the last to make it from raw milk, and visitors can tour the workshops, watch a film, look over the old equipment and taste before buying.
new.tip: Locals eat it on bread with a spoon of sirop de Liège to soften the bite. Ring ahead before you set out to check visiting times.
new.q: La Fromagerie du Vieux Moulin Sur la Commune 14 Herve

new.title: Toast the Fagnes at Belgium's highest brewery
new.desc: Belgium Peak Beer brews in Sourbrodt, a short way from the Signal de Botrange, the highest point in the country. Its blonde, brune, triple and blueberry beers are made with water from the Hautes Fagnes and poured in a brasserie whose terrace looks out over the moor.
new.tip: Several waymarked walks from 2.5 to 12 km start at the door, so earn your glass first. Parking is hard to find on busy days.
new.q: Belgium Peak Beer Rue de Botrange 123 Sourbrodt

new.title: Share a baiser de Malmedy on the main square
new.desc: The baiser, or kiss, is Malmedy's own pastry: two meringue shells stuck together with whipped cream, said to have been invented in the mid 19th century by the pastry cook Rodolphe Wiertz. The Halmes bakery on Place Albert Ier is a favourite address for them, along with its blueberry tarts.
new.tip: They are fragile and the cream does not travel, so eat them on the spot or buy them last thing before going home.
new.q: Halmes Place Albert Ier Malmedy

new.title: Pay your respects at the Fort de Loncin
new.desc: Loncin was one of twelve concrete forts built around Liège between 1888 and 1891 to General Brialmont's plans. At the start of the First World War a shell set off a huge explosion that buried most of the defenders, who still lie under the rubble; the fort is a national necropolis and, since 2023, part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of First World War memorial sites.
new.tip: Nothing was rebuilt after the blast, which is what makes the visit so striking. Check opening days before you go and allow a couple of hours.
new.q: Fort de Loncin Rue des Héros 15 Ans

new.title: Walk across the Gileppe dam in the Hertogenwald
new.desc: The Gileppe dam, in the eastern part of the Hertogenwald forest, is one of the oldest gravity dams in Europe. It was designed by the Liège engineer Eugène Bidaut and inaugurated by King Leopold II on 28 July 1878, and a monumental stone lion sits on its crest.
new.tip: Walk across the top of the dam to stand under the lion, then take one of the forest paths along the lake. Come on a weekday for quiet.
new.q: Barrage de la Gileppe Jalhay

new.title: Roam the ruined castle of Franchimont
new.desc: This 11th century fortress stands on a spur above the Hoëgne valley at Theux and was an important stronghold of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège until it was demilitarised in the 17th century. Since 1967 a group of volunteers, the Compagnons de Franchimont, have been clearing and restoring the ruins.
new.tip: The castle is open in the daytime from April to October. Wear sturdy shoes, as the ground inside the walls is rough.
new.q: Château de Franchimont Theux

new.title: Soak above the town at the Thermes de Spa
new.desc: The town that gave its name to every spa in the world still takes the waters, now in a modern bath house on the hill of Annette et Lubin above the centre. Indoor and outdoor pools are filled with warm mineral water, with saunas and steam rooms alongside.
new.tip: A funicular climbs to the baths from the centre of town. Weekday mornings are the calmest time to go.
new.q: Les Thermes de Spa Colline d'Annette et Lubin Spa

new.title: Float through the Grottes de Remouchamps by boat
new.desc: The caves of Remouchamps were carved over more than a million years by an underground river, the Rubicon, which first hollowed out an upper gallery and then found a lower way. You visit one gallery on foot and the other by boat on the river itself, a trip that has earned the caves the nickname the Marvel of Marvels.
new.tip: It is cool and damp underground all year, so bring a sweater even in August. The entrance is in the village, close to the Amblève.
new.q: Grottes de Remouchamps Aywaille

new.title: Join the Cwarmê, the carnival of Malmedy
new.desc: Malmedy's carnival, the Cwarmê, runs for four days up to midnight on Shrove Tuesday and was first recorded in 1459. Although the town lies in the East Cantons, it is a thoroughly Walloon and Latin carnival, and it peaks on Sunday afternoon with the great costumed parade through the centre.
new.tip: Sunday is the day to come. The masked figures love to tease bystanders, so play along, wear old clothes and arrive early to find parking.
new.q: Place Albert Ier Malmedy
